6 x 3 ft mats in rows, 1 ft inset and edge clearance, gaps 2/1.5/1 ft never below 1 ft, each nudged/turned by a positional draw and kept only where its outline stays 0.1 ft clear of every neighbor's; count in [ceil(full/3), floor(2 full/3)] with an even thinning; rows a GUESS, thinning and nudge a CONVENTION.
decisions.why: The 1 ft least gap and the hand-laid turn serve the GM's stated aim that the drawn mats read as mats ('we can't render dozens of mats and have that be legible'); settlement-reviews 4-6 read 0.5 ft as paving. Matches yards.py (MAT_GAPS_FT = (2.0, 1.5, 1.0), MAT_INK_CLEAR_FT 0.1, _lay_by_hand).

decisions.summary: A yard that physically cannot hold a third of a full cover at a 1 ft gap draws as many as fit at it, at any size.
decisions.why: Extends the round-3 ruling: the one-third floor is this project's proxy, not the GM's number, and holding it where a third cannot fit at the least legible gap defeats the GM's own purpose (legible mats giving the impression of many). The 400 sq ft bound was itself a proxy for 'cannot fit'. Measured this round: of the pool's short yards only Inashiro's 20 x 14 ft yard is in this class (4 fit, 4 drawn).

decisions.summary: 'Cannot reach a third at 1 ft' decided by the one centered lattice mat_cells lays per gap step (the best of 2/1.5/1), with no search for a placement that fits more.
decisions.why: Excuses yards that CAN hold a third at 1 ft. Measured on the working-tree SVGs 2026-09-28 with a shifted unturned 1 ft-gap lattice (corners 1 ft inside the drawn outline, off the rack): eight of nine short yards hold a third - Kashikawa 22 x 15 ft draws 3 where 6 fit, Sawada 31 x 22 ft 8 where 12, Mizuguchi 10 and 11 where 12 and 15, Sawada's others 6/7/7/3 where 7/9/8/6. The cause is the centered lattice (e.g. three 1 ft columns whose outer two fall off a 22 ft floor, where two columns fit). 'The literal reading is harder to implement' is not a ground; the exception's own words are 'cannot hold', and the mechanism must find what fits before drawing fewer than a third.

decisions.summary: The short-yard floor lowered from four mats to three.
decisions.why: No measured yard holds fewer than four at a 1 ft gap (the smallest, Inashiro's 20 x 14 ft, holds 4; Sawada's 20 x 14 ft with a rack holds 6). Three exists only on the two yards where the centered lattice draws half of what fits, so the floor was lowered to fit the mechanism's shortfall, not a physical limit; and three mats weakens the GM's 'render a bunch of mats over the yard'. Keep four unless a rolled yard is measured that cannot hold four.
